label: Environmental response (oil and hazardous releases)
description: The people who manage a release of oil or a hazardous substance: a responsible party's incident management team (the older plans call it the spill management team), its qualified individual and response contractors, the Coast Guard or EPA On-Scene Coordinator and the Area Committee in a unified command, the state agencies, and the water utilities and wildlife agencies downstream.

vocabulary.facility: the source of the release (a vessel, terminal, tank farm, pipeline or platform) and the response organization built around it
vocabulary.public: shoreline communities, fishers, boaters, water customers and the people near the plume
vocabulary.frontline: OSRO crews, boom and skimmer operators, wildlife responders, shoreline survey teams, vessel masters, terminal operators, field engineers
vocabulary.operationsCenter: the Incident Command Post and the unified command, with the Joint Information Center

it: the Incident Command Post network and the unified command board (WebEOC style)
ERMA or a similar common operational picture
the trajectory model and the oil weathering model run by the Scientific Support Coordinator
ICS forms and the incident action plan
resource tracking for boom, skimmers, boats and aircraft
email, a claims system and the Joint Information Center website
ot: pipeline SCADA with leak detection and remote valves (at the source)
tank gauging and transfer system shutdown
vessel tracking (AIS) and vessel traffic service
tide, current and wind sensors and buoys
intake and treatment SCADA at a downstream water utility

roles.name: Qualified Individual
roles.description: Has full authority to activate the plan and contract resources; makes the first notifications and activates the OSRO.

roles.name: Federal On-Scene Coordinator
roles.description: Coast Guard or EPA; directs the federal response and decides on countermeasures with the Regional Response Team.

roles.name: State On-Scene Coordinator
roles.description: Sets state priorities, wildlife and fishery closures in state waters.

roles.name: Responsible Party Incident Commander
roles.description: Commits company resources and cost; proposes strategies to the unified command.

roles.name: Operations Section Chief
roles.description: Owns the tactical plan: source control, containment, recovery, shoreline cleanup, wildlife, burning and dispersant operations.

roles.name: Planning Section Chief
roles.description: Owns the incident action plan, the situation picture, the trajectory forecasts and the next operational period's plan.

roles.name: Environmental Unit Leader
roles.description: Ranks sensitive areas and resources at risk, tracks permits and consultations, waste plan and sampling.

roles.name: Scientific Support Coordinator
roles.description: NOAA advisor to the FOSC for trajectories, weathering, resources at risk and the trade-offs of countermeasures.

roles.name: Logistics Section Chief
roles.description: Supplies boom, boats, aircraft, staging, vessels of opportunity, personnel and lodging.

roles.name: Finance/Administration Section Chief
roles.description: Tracks cost and claims and the interface with the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund.

roles.name: Safety Officer
roles.description: Owns the site safety plan, air monitoring, heat stress, vessel and aircraft safety.

roles.name: Public Information Officer (Joint Information Center)
roles.description: Joint Information Center messages, community meetings, the claims line, fishing and recreation advisories.

roles.name: Wildlife Branch Director
roles.description: Hazing, capture, stabilization and rehabilitation of wildlife with the permits of the state and the Fish and Wildlife Service.

roles.name: OSRO Duty Manager
roles.description: The response contractor's duty manager: equipment, crews, skimmers and boom named in the plan.

outsideParties: the Coast Guard Sector and Captain of the Port
NOAA Office of Response and Restoration
the US Fish and Wildlife Service
the state fish and wildlife agency
mediaChannels: local TV with aerial footage of the slick
photos of oiled birds and shorelines on social media
national outlets for a large release

sceneAnchors.public: a coastal town waterfront with a boat ramp and fishing boats, residents at a rope barrier watching, a hazy sky
sceneAnchors.control: an incident command post in a conference room: a wall map of a bay with boom positions, section chiefs at laptops, an ICS organization chart on a whiteboard
sceneAnchors.exterior: a marsh shoreline with orange boom in the water, a work boat and responders in coveralls and life vests, overcast sky

addedThreatFamilies.label: Vessel casualty with cargo or fuel release
addedThreatFamilies.description: A grounding, collision or hull failure releases cargo or bunker fuel into a waterway; the vessel owner's qualified individual, the salvors and the Coast Guard form a unified command.

phaseArc.title: Discovery and Notification
phaseArc.goal: Notice reaches the right people in the right order: the vessel reports, the qualified individual activates the plan, the National Response Center is called.
beats: The master reports a grounding and a sheen to the Coast Guard Sector
The qualified individual finds the vessel response plan and the salvage and OSRO contract numbers
A first overflight finds more sheen than the vessel reported

phaseArc.title: Activation and Unified Command
phaseArc.goal: A unified command forms from three agencies with different priorities; the casualty and the spill compete for resources.
beats: The Coast Guard asks for a command post and an Incident Commander from the owner
Salvage wants to refloat; the FOSC wants a stability assessment first
The OSRO reports only half the plan's equipment is within the response time

phaseArc.title: Trajectory and Protection
phaseArc.goal: The trajectory forecast and the sensitive-area ranking drive where the first boom goes; the clock is landfall.
beats: The Scientific Support Coordinator delivers a 24 and 48 hour trajectory with an uncertainty envelope
Two sensitive areas cannot both be protected with the boom on hand
Wind shifts and the forecast moves landfall earlier
A countermeasure request must be decided before the weather closes the window

phaseArc.title: Recovery and Demobilization
phaseArc.goal: Recovery, shoreline cleanup and claims run into the next operational periods and the Hot Wash.
beats: Lightering reduces the remaining cargo risk
Shoreline assessment teams report oiling and the cleanup endpoint is argued
A fishing closure and a claims line are announced

decisionPointExamples: commit the limited boom to the marsh or to the water intake
ask for dispersant now or wait for the next forecast
lighten the vessel before the weather turns or hold to avoid a larger release
close a shipping channel and accept the port delay
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a pilot report, an overflight sheen, a tank sounding, a stability calculation, a vessel tracking position, a sample result
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: boom or boats not where the plan says, weather closing the window, a salvage plan that conflicts with the recovery plan, a vessel of opportunity not cleared for oil work
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the Coast Guard Captain of the Port as Federal On-Scene Coordinator, the state, and the salvage master
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Worst case discharge for a vessel means its entire cargo in adverse weather; do not use the facility sense. Quantities in barrels or gallons, never mixed in one document.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Facility or tank release
addedThreatFamilies.description: A tank, pipe or transfer failure at a terminal or plant releases oil or a hazardous liquid that reaches secondary containment, a drain or the water.

phaseArc.title: Discovery and Notification
phaseArc.goal: The release is found and reported inside the facility's own clock; the qualified individual decides what is reportable.
beats: An operator finds product in the dike and the sump alarm is inhibited
The qualified individual and the OSRO are called before the volume is known
The first volume estimate is revised upward

phaseArc.title: Activation and Unified Command
phaseArc.goal: The facility's incident management team stands up and the federal and state coordinators join.
beats: The facility response plan names the team and the equipment
An outside responder asks who has authority to commit contractors
The fire department and the environmental team disagree on foam use

phaseArc.title: Trajectory and Protection
phaseArc.goal: Containment inside the facility fails or holds; the sensitive area downstream sets the priority.
beats: A drain valve left open let product reach a ditch
Rain threatens to overflow the containment
The facility asks to use a chemical agent or burn

phaseArc.title: Recovery and Demobilization
phaseArc.goal: Cleanup, waste handling and the plan review follow.
beats: Waste manifests and storage for recovered product
The regulator asks for the exercise and drill records
The plan's worst case discharge volume is questioned

decisionPointExamples: divert product to a second tank or accept the risk of overflowing the dike
let the fire burn or cool the tank and spread foam runoff
open the dike to the ditch to protect the tank farm
shut down the neighboring unit
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a gauge reading, a sump alarm, a dike inspection, a drain valve line-up, an operator log entry
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a transfer pump that will not start, a vacuum truck stuck in the mud, a drain valve that cannot be closed, waste storage full
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the state environmental agency and the Coast Guard or EPA On-Scene Coordinator
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: A facility's worst case discharge is the volume stated in its plan, not the largest conceivable; compare the exercise volume with the plan volume.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Pipeline release to a river or wetland
addedThreatFamilies.description: A hazardous liquid pipeline releases crude or product into a creek or river; the oil travels downstream faster than the response forms.

phaseArc.title: Discovery and Notification
phaseArc.goal: A leak is recognized late; the control room, field crew and a member of the public each hold a piece.
beats: A pressure drop and a landowner call arrive minutes apart
The control room restarts the line after an alarm
The first caller to the National Response Center is a neighbor, not the operator

phaseArc.title: Activation and Unified Command
phaseArc.goal: The operator isolates the line, activates the plan and joins a unified command with the state.
beats: Valve closure is confirmed in the field
The estimated volume is argued: the model, the meter and the field disagree
Local responders ask what is in the product

phaseArc.title: Trajectory and Protection
phaseArc.goal: Travel time to the downstream intake and the nearest wetland sets the clock; upstream and downstream teams split.
beats: The river gauge shows a rise that speeds the oil
The water utility asks for a time and a concentration
Boom held by a bridge or a dam changes the plan
A town 20 miles down asks to be told

phaseArc.title: Recovery and Demobilization
phaseArc.goal: Recovery in a river, sampling, waste, restoration and the investigation.
beats: Sunken or submerged oil complicates recovery
The regulator opens an investigation of leak detection
The operator's response plan is reviewed within 30 days of a change in the worst case discharge

decisionPointExamples: restart the line to find out whether the leak is real
close the downstream intake early and lose supply, or wait for more certainty
open a dam gate to flush the river or hold the oil behind it
ask to burn oil on the river
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a pressure trend, a pump trip, a landowner call, a smell report, a gauge rise, a field valve status
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a closed road to the valve site, boom that cannot be set in current above a set speed, ice, a landowner who denies access
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the downstream water utility, the state, and the pipeline regulator
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Leak recognition belongs in the pipeline control room exercise; the spill response starts when someone calls. Gauge readings and arrival estimates carry uncertainty.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Offshore release
addedThreatFamilies.description: A platform, pipeline or well releases oil offshore; response depends on aircraft, vessels and source control more than shore teams.

phaseArc.title: Discovery and Notification
phaseArc.goal: The operator and the regulator get word through different channels; volume is uncertain.
beats: A sheen reported by a supply boat captain
The source control team asks for the well plan
The first estimate of flow rate is a range, not a number

phaseArc.title: Activation and Unified Command
phaseArc.goal: The operator's team, the Coast Guard, the offshore regulator and the state form a unified command; source control is the top objective.
beats: The operator wants to focus on the well, the state on the shore
Aircraft and vessels for dispersant application are queued behind other uses

phaseArc.title: Trajectory and Protection
phaseArc.goal: Offshore recovery and dispersants against a shoreline clock; the forecast is a cone, not a line.
beats: Winds hold the slick offshore for a day, then turn
Subsea dispersant use requires a decision with limited data
Fishers ask for compensation before closure

phaseArc.title: Recovery and Demobilization
phaseArc.goal: Long operations; the demobilization question: when is it done?
beats: Shoreline assessment endpoints
A natural resource trustee asks to join sampling

decisionPointExamples: approve a countermeasure with incomplete monitoring data
move equipment from one coast to another
pull vessels off station in a storm
declare a closure of the whole fishing area
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a platform status report, a flow estimate, a satellite sheen detection, a pressure reading
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: distance and weather that stop boats, aircraft in short supply, a tool that fails in the well
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the offshore regulator and the Coast Guard, with the state for the shore
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Offshore volumes are large and uncertain; state ranges. Operator, regulator and Coast Guard each own different decisions.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Chemical release with a toxic plume
addedThreatFamilies.description: A chemical release produces a vapor cloud as well as a liquid spill; air monitoring and protective action decisions run alongside the water response.

phaseArc.title: Discovery and Notification
phaseArc.goal: A release is reported with an unknown product; the plant, 911 and a driver each name it differently.
beats: The shipping paper and the placard disagree
The plant reports an off-site odor

phaseArc.title: Activation and Unified Command
phaseArc.goal: Incident command and the response organization share a unified command; air monitoring starts.
beats: The fire department hazmat team asks for the product data sheet
Spill and plume responsibilities blur

phaseArc.title: Trajectory and Protection
phaseArc.goal: The plume footprint and the wind drive the shelter or evacuate decision; the spill drains to a creek.
beats: Concentration readings at the fence line disagree with the model
A school sits inside the yellow zone
The wind shifts toward a nursing home

phaseArc.title: Recovery and Demobilization
phaseArc.goal: All clear, re-entry and the water-side cleanup.
beats: Clearance sampling
A community meeting demands answers

decisionPointExamples: shelter in place or evacuate a neighborhood
close a road and a rail line for how long
open the spill to the creek or hold it on site
tell the downstream intake now or after sampling
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a monitor reading, a shipping paper, a placard, an odor complaint, a wind shift on the site met tower
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a monitor that fails, a wind forecast that changes, a product name that is wrong on the paper
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the fire department hazmat team and county emergency management
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Footprints are zones by concentration level for a stated product, wind and time; label every figure as an exercise model, not a forecast.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Marine firefighting and salvage
addedThreatFamilies.description: A vessel fire or casualty with cargo at risk: firefighting, stability, lightering and the spill that may follow.

phaseArc.title: Discovery and Notification
phaseArc.goal: The fire and the potential spill are reported together; responders cannot yet tell which comes first.
beats: The vessel reports fire in an engine room
The port requests a firefighting vessel

phaseArc.title: Activation and Unified Command
phaseArc.goal: Command is shared among the fire service, the Coast Guard, the owner and the salvor.
beats: Water used to fight the fire affects stability
A salvage plan needs agency approval

phaseArc.title: Trajectory and Protection
phaseArc.goal: Trade-offs between the fire, stability and the oil; the sensitive area is a wetland near the berth.
beats: The vessel lists after firefighting water
Boom is placed before the fire is out

phaseArc.title: Recovery and Demobilization
phaseArc.goal: Removal of the vessel, lightering and cleanup.
beats: The salvage master and the FOSC disagree on the tow route

decisionPointExamples: keep fighting the fire and risk stability or hold and risk the cargo
tow into the port or anchor outside
sacrifice a berth or a channel
burn off or lighter the cargo
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a stability calculation, a draft reading, a thermal image, a firefighter report
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: firefighting vessels busy elsewhere, a berth not available, weather that stops lightering
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the port authority, the pilots, the fire service and the salvor
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Fire, stability and spill decisions are made by different people at once; show the dependencies.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Drinking water intake threatened
addedThreatFamilies.description: A release upstream or along a coast threatens a drinking water intake; the utility, the response organization and the health agency each own part of the decision.

phaseArc.title: Discovery and Notification
phaseArc.goal: The utility learns of the release by phone from a third party; time to arrival is the first number needed.
beats: A regional news alert reaches the utility before the operator's call
The utility asks for the product and a time

phaseArc.title: Activation and Unified Command
phaseArc.goal: The utility joins the unified command through a liaison; the health agency is brought in.
beats: The utility's plan lists a closure trigger
The state drinking water program and the response organization disagree on the trigger

phaseArc.title: Trajectory and Protection
phaseArc.goal: The closure decision against the arrival estimate and the storage on hand.
beats: Storage covers 36 hours at normal demand
The model gives arrival between 2200 and 0200
An exclusion boom is placed at the intake

phaseArc.title: Recovery and Demobilization
phaseArc.goal: Reopening depends on sampling; the public asks when the water is safe.
beats: Sample results arrive in batches
The state sets the reopening criteria

decisionPointExamples: close the intake on the early arrival estimate or on the sample
issue a do-not-drink advisory or only a conservation request
switch to an alternate source that costs more and is lower quality
reopen on a clean sample or wait for three
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a gauge, a trajectory run, a sample result, a hotline call, a boom position report
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a valve that will not close, an alternate source with a different chemistry, a lab backlog
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the water utility, the state drinking water program and the unified command
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: The utility decides to close its intake; the response organization advises with a time and a confidence. Use arrival windows, not a single time.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Wildlife and sensitive shoreline impact
addedThreatFamilies.description: Oil reaches a nesting area, a marsh or a recreational beach; wildlife, shoreline cleanup and public pressure dominate.

phaseArc.title: Discovery and Notification
phaseArc.goal: First oiled animals or oil on the shore are reported by the public before the response knows.
beats: A beachgoer posts a photo of an oiled bird
The wildlife hotline overloads

phaseArc.title: Activation and Unified Command
phaseArc.goal: Wildlife and shoreline branches are set up with permits; volunteers arrive.
beats: Untrained volunteers handle oiled animals
A state agency asks to stop the hazing

phaseArc.title: Trajectory and Protection
phaseArc.goal: Protecting the marsh or the beach, and the trade-off of cleanup damage.
beats: Heavy cleanup in a marsh would harm the nesting birds
The tide and the wind move the oil

phaseArc.title: Recovery and Demobilization
phaseArc.goal: Endpoints, restoration and trustees.
beats: The cleanup endpoint is negotiated
A natural resource trustee begins an assessment

decisionPointExamples: clean now and damage the habitat, or leave the oil to weather
haze birds from the area or leave them
close a beach during a holiday weekend
accept volunteers or turn them away
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a SCAT survey, a wildlife count, an overflight observation, a photo from the public
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: permits not in place, a rehabilitation facility full, a tide that blocks access
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the state wildlife agency, the Fish and Wildlife Service and the natural resource trustees
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Only permitted responders handle wildlife; keep volunteers at the registration step. Cleanup can do more harm than the oil in some habitats.

noiseExamples: a boater asking whether the bay is open
a contractor asking for a vessel of opportunity rate
a reporter asking for a tour of the staging area
a volunteer offering a boat without a safety course
a vendor offering a new sorbent product
pressureExamples: a fisher's video of black water at the dock with thousands of shares
a county commissioner demanding the volume figure now
a wildlife group saying responders are late
a utility manager asking for a firm arrival time the model cannot give
a state official asking for a different strategy than the federal coordinator
agencyPattern: NOAA|NRC|National Response Center|Coast Guard|Captain of the Port|Regional Response Team|RRT|Fish and Wildlife|PHMSA|BSEE|EPA
